question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

args.question: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim for compensation for death of her husband (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000) in a road accident involving a commercial truck driven without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability on ground that the policy is void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The insurer must pay third-party compensation and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim of a commercial vehicle accident. The driver lacked a valid licence/endorsement for the commercial vehicle — directly analogous to the licence deficiency in Iyyapan.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court judgment is the strongest binding authority. It squarely holds that even where the driver of a commercial vehicle lacks the proper licence/endorsement, the insurer's statutory liability to third parties remains intact, with a right of recovery against the insured.
supporting.quote: Reading the provisions of Sections 146 and 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is evidently clear that in certain circumstances the insurer's right is safeguarded but in any event the insurer has to pay compensation when a valid certificate of insurance is issued notwithstanding the fact that the insurer may proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149 MV Act. Even if the insurer proves a conscious breach of policy terms (invalid driving licence), it must pay the third party first and can recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased were third parties travelling in a goods vehicle. The driver had an invalid licence. The court directed pay-and-recover despite the breach being established.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment comprehensively reviews the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the statutory liability to third parties overrides policy breaches. It directly counters the insurer's argument that proving breach absolves it.
supporting.quote: There is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks the appropriate endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle (having only an LMV/transport endorsement), the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The offending vehicle was a heavy goods lorry; the driver held only an LMV licence without the specific endorsement. The deceased was a third party. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is factually on all fours — a commercial goods vehicle, a driver without the correct licence for that class of vehicle, and a third-party death. The court applied Swaran Singh and Iyyapan to order pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held an LMV licence but drove a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle) without the required badge/authorisation. The claimant was a third party. Pay-and-recover was ordered.
supporting.why_it_matters: This case confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves breach (driver not 'duly licensed' for the specific vehicle class), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration, when the claimant is a third party.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent — Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired at the time of the accident. The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights against the insured.
supporting.why_it_matters: This case reinforces that even a lapsed/expired licence (functionally equivalent to 'no valid licence') does not allow the insurer to escape third-party liability. The ratio extends to any licence defect short of a fake licence where the owner was complicit.
supporting.quote: The liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant in the first instance and recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.

args.question: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim for compensation for death of her husband (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000) in a road accident involving a commercial truck driven without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability on ground that the policy is void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle. The insurer must pay third-party compensation and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim of a commercial vehicle accident. The driver lacked a valid licence/endorsement for the commercial vehicle — directly analogous to the licence deficiency in Iyyapan.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court judgment is the strongest binding authority. It squarely holds that even where the driver of a commercial vehicle lacks the proper licence/endorsement, the insurer's statutory liability to third parties remains intact, with a right of recovery against the insured.
supporting.quote: the insurer has to pay to the third parties only on account of the fact that a policy of insurance has been issued in respect of the vehicle, but the insurer is entitled to recover any such sum from the insured if the insurer were not otherwise liable to pay such sum to the insured by virtue of the conditions of the contract of insurance indicated by the policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149 MV Act. Even if the insurer proves a conscious breach of policy terms (invalid driving licence), it must pay the third party first and can recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased were third parties. The driver had an invalid licence. The court directed pay-and-recover despite the breach being established.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment comprehensively reviews the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Swaran Singh) and confirms that the statutory liability to third parties overrides policy breaches. It directly counters the insurer's argument that proving breach absolves it.
supporting.quote: there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks the appropriate endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The offending vehicle was a heavy goods lorry; the driver held only an LMV licence without the specific endorsement. The deceased was a third party. The court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is factually on all fours — a commercial goods vehicle, a driver without the correct licence for that class of vehicle, and a third-party death. The court applied Swaran Singh and Iyyapan to order pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held an LMV licence but drove a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle) without the required badge/authorisation. The claimant was a third party. Pay-and-recover was ordered.
supporting.why_it_matters: This case confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves breach (driver not 'duly licensed' for the specific vehicle class), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration, when the claimant is a third party.
supporting.quote: in view of the decision of NATIONAL INSURANCE COMPANY LTD. VS. SWARAN SINGH AND OTHERS (2004) 3 SCC 297 and reiterated in other decisions we are of the view that the Appellant - insurer must pay the amount to the claimant - 1st Respondent and then recover the same from the insured

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy a third-party award regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired at the time of the accident. The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights against the insured.
supporting.why_it_matters: This case reinforces that even a lapsed/expired licence (functionally equivalent to 'no valid licence') does not allow the insurer to escape third-party liability.
supporting.quote: the liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy and any breach of conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant in the first instance and recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The charge sheet confirmed the absence of a licence. The tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match — the driver held NO licence whatsoever (not merely the wrong class). Despite this being a 'fundamental breach', the tribunal applied Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Amrit Paul Singh to order pay-and-recover, confirming that third-party rights are paramount.
supporting.quote: the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the offending tanker had no valid licence. The court upheld the pay-and-recover order while also enhancing compensation.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Allahabad High Court judgment directly rejects the insurer's argument that proving absence of a licence absolves it. It confirms that the insurer's remedy is recovery, not avoidance.
supporting.quote: The Hon'ble Supreme Court vide its judgment rendered in the case of S. Iyyapan (supra) has categorically held that if the driver of the vehicle does not possess valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further it can recover the amount of compensation from the insured i.e. owner of the vehicle.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be based on the deceased's age (not the claimants'), future prospects apply to self-employed/fixed-salary individuals, and courts must award just compensation.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a fixed-salary employee. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles: future prospects based on age, multiplier based on deceased's age, and standardised deductions.
supporting.why_it_matters: This provides the quantum framework. For a 42-year-old self-employed deceased, 25% future prospects (Pranay Sethi), multiplier of 14 (Sarla Verma), and 1/3rd deduction for 3 dependants apply.
supporting.quote: We therefore hold that the multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in column (4) of the Table above (prepared by applying Susamma Thomas, Trilok Chandra and Charlie), which starts with an operative multiplier of 18... M-14 for 41 to 45 years

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is not valid on the date of accident, the insurer must still pay the third-party award and recover from the insured under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired and was renewed only after the accident. The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover from the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Karnataka High Court judgment confirms that even where the driver had no valid licence on the accident date, the third-party claimant must be paid first. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not the claimant.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and has no application to own-damage claims or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this case to argue that Swaran Singh's 'pay and recover' principle is limited. However, the case expressly states: 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Our client IS a third party, so this case actually confirms our position. The risk is low because the case draws a boundary that excludes our facts from the limitation.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly holds that for third-party risks, the insurer must indemnify and recover. The case is about own-damage claims and fake licences — neither of which applies here. Our client is a third-party claimant, squarely within the protected category.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger travels in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and pay-and-recover cannot be invoked.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may try to analogise that the deceased here was not a 'third party' either. However, this case is about a gratuitous passenger in a private vehicle — entirely different from a pedestrian/other road user killed by a commercial truck. The deceased here is a paradigmatic third party.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns passengers in a private vehicle used for hire — a coverage exclusion, not a licence breach. Our deceased was a third-party road user (not an occupant of the insured vehicle), which is the core class protected by Section 147. The case is factually inapposite.
adverse.quote: when the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover'

priority_arguments: 1. Statutory liability under Section 149 MV Act: The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided by proving a breach of policy conditions. The insurer must pay first and recover from the insured (relying on S. Iyyapan v. United India Insurance, Satto v. New India Assurance, and Chennamma).

2. The deceased was a third-party road user: Unlike gratuitous passengers or own-damage claimants, the deceased was a pedestrian/other road user — the exact class of persons the compulsory insurance regime is designed to protect.

3. Even total absence of a licence does not defeat third-party claims: Sunil Shreesail Killiket (driver with no licence at all) and Meena (driver with no valid licence) both ordered pay-and-recover. The insurer's remedy is against the owner, not the claimant.

4. Quantum under Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, income Rs 35,000/month. Apply 25% future prospects, multiplier 14, 1/3rd deduction for 3 dependants. Total compensation ~Rs 51 lakh plus conventional heads and interest.
5. No contributory negligence: The truck driver was solely negligent. The burden of proving contributory negligence is on the insurer.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition until realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the compute_quantum tool under the Pranay Sethi/Sarla Verma framework: Monthly income Rs 35,000; age 42 (self-employed); 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Future prospects: +25% (self-employed, age 42). Deduction: 1/3rd (3 dependants). Multiplier: 14. Loss of dependency: Rs 49,00,000. Conventional heads: Rs 1,99,650 (estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 79,860 + parental consortium Rs 79,860 for two minor children). Total: ~Rs 51,00,000.
risks: 1. The insurer may argue that the total absence of a licence is a 'fundamental breach' that goes beyond mere non-endorsement. However, the corpus consistently holds that even fundamental breach only entitles the insurer to recovery rights, not exoneration from third-party liability.

2. The insurer may attempt to prove that the owner/transport company was complicit in employing an unlicensed driver, arguing 'conscious breach.' Even if proved, the remedy remains pay-and-recover (Satto).

3. If the insurer proves the licence was fake (not merely absent), and that the owner knew or ought to have known, the position remains the same for third-party claims — pay-and-recover (Swaran Singh, para 105, as cited in Satto).

4. Quantum could be contested on the nature of employment (self-employed vs. permanent). If the deceased was in permanent employment, 30% future prospects apply instead of 25%, which would increase the award — this is a favourable risk.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the accident location. Seek: (a) declaration that the insurer is jointly and severally liable with the owner/driver; (b) pay-and-recover order against the insurer; (c) compensation of ~Rs 51 lakh with interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition; (d) separate heads for spousal consortium (Rs 79,860 for the widow) and parental consortium (Rs 79,860 for each minor child) under Magma General v. Nanu Ram and Satinder Kaur.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment that exonerates an insurer from third-party liability solely on the ground that the driver held no licence at all. Every relevant case in the corpus orders pay-and-recover. This is a favourable finding.

The corpus contains no judgment directly on point where the deceased was a pedestrian/other road user killed by a commercial truck with a completely unlicensed driver — but the principles from the analogous cases (Sunil Shreesail Killiket, Meena, Chennamma) uniformly support our position.

The quantum computation assumes self-employment. If the deceased was in permanent employment, the future prospects addition would be 30% (not 25%), yielding a higher award. Counsel should verify the deceased's employment status.

The corpus does not contain any judgment from the Supreme Court on the specific question of whether 'no licence at all' for a commercial vehicle is treated differently from 'wrong class of licence' for third-party claims. The tribunal-level and High Court judgments in the corpus treat them identically for pay-and-recover purposes.

Doc_006 (Meena) cites United India Insurance v. Sujata Arora which held that driving without a licence or with a fake licence completely exonerates the insurer. However, the same court in Meena then followed the later Supreme Court judgment in Iyyapan which overrides Sujata Arora on this point. Counsel should be aware of this tension and be prepared to argue that Iyyapan (2013) being later in time and from the Supreme Court prevails over Sujata Arora (also 2013).
